name: Gowdy Cosmologies
description: Closed vacuum universes holding gravitational waves that travel along one direction, with two commuting spacelike Killing vectors and space $T^3$, $S^3$, or $S^2 \times S^1$. Einstein's equations for them reduce to two coupled wave equations in one space dimension and a quadrature, and near the singularity each point of space approaches a Kasner universe of its own.
convention: Every coordinate is a pure number and the length $L$ carries the dimensions, so no factor of $c$ appears. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: Robert Gowdy took the cylindrical gravitational waves of Albert Einstein and Nathan Rosen in 1971 and changed their boundary conditions: "New boundary conditions on the Einstein-Rosen-Bondi gravitational-wave metrics yield closed inhomogeneous universes which solve Einstein's vacuum field equations exactly" [gowdy1971]. By 1974 he had classified the vacuum spacetimes with two commuting spacelike Killing vectors and compact invariant hypersurfaces, and showed that space must be $T^3$, $S^3$, or $S^2 \times S^1$ [gowdy1974, garfinkle1999]. Charles Misner took the torus in 1973 as his example of a minisuperspace and called it "an exact vacuum solution of Einstein's equations representing gravitational waves propagating in an expanding closed universe" [misner1973gowdy].¶Each orbit of the two Killing vectors is a closed surface of area $4\pi^2L^2R$, with $L$ a constant length, and in a vacuum $R$ obeys the wave equation $\partial_\theta^2R - \partial_t^2R = 0$ [gowdy2014]. The solution $R = t$ with $\theta$ periodic is the torus, which expands from $t = 0$, and $R = \sin t\sin\theta$ is $S^3$ and $S^2 \times S^1$, which expand from $t = 0$ and collapse at $t = \pi$ [gowdy2014]. The wave amplitudes $P$ and $Q$ obey two coupled wave equations in which the third metric function does not appear, and that function follows from them by an integral [gowdy2014]. With $Q = 0$, the polarised case, the equation for $P$ is linear [gowdy2014]. Where the gradient of $R$ is spacelike, the $S^3$ and $S^2 \times S^1$ universes are locally Einstein-Rosen waves [gowdy2014].¶On the torus the solution $P = \tau$, $Q = 0$, with $\tau = -\ln t$, is the flat Kasner universe [ringstrom2010]. The Taub universe is a Gowdy spacetime on $S^3$ [gowdy2014]. Octavio Obregón and Michael Ryan noted in 1998 that the Kerr metric between its outer and inner horizons is a Gowdy spacetime on $S^2 \times S^1$ [obregon1998, garfinkle1999]. Gowdy wrote in 2014 that the spacetimes "are not legitimate cosmological models because their matter content is limited to massless fields and their $G_2$ symmetry is quite special" [gowdy2014].¶Vladimir Belinskii, Isaak Khalatnikov, and Evgenii Lifshitz argued in 1970 that near a generic singularity spatial gradients become unimportant and each small region of space evolves as a homogeneous anisotropic universe of its own, oscillating infinitely many times [bkl1970, gowdy2014]. Douglas Eardley, Edison Liang, and Rainer Sachs named a singularity velocity dominated in 1972 when the terms of Einstein's equations with spatial derivatives can be neglected near it [eardley1972, berger1993]. Beverly Berger showed in 1974 that a polarised solution on the torus with $P \to v\tau$ approaches a Kasner universe whose parameter $v$ differs at each $\theta$ [berger1974, berger1993]. Vincent Moncrief proved in 1981 that the areal time $t$ of a vacuum torus runs over the whole of $(0, \infty)$ and that its surfaces of constant $t$ cover the maximal globally hyperbolic development [moncrief1981, ringstrom2010]. James Isenberg and Moncrief proved in 1990 that every polarised solution converges toward the singularity to a solution of the equations with the spatial derivatives dropped, $P = v(\theta)\tau + \phi(\theta)$ [isenberg1990, ringstrom2010]. With Piotr Chruściel they proved the same year that, for an open dense set of polarised initial data on $T^3$, $S^3$, or $S^2 \times S^1$, the maximal development is inextendible, which is Roger Penrose's strong cosmic censorship for that class [chrusciel1990cim, penrose1969, ringstrom2010].¶For the unpolarised torus, Boro Grubišić and Moncrief derived formal expansions about the singularity in 1993 and conjectured the same velocity dominated approach [grubisic1993, berger1993, ringstrom2010]. Berger and Moncrief integrated the equations numerically that year and found support for the conjecture with $v < 1$, together with "a new phenomenon of the development of small scale spatial structure" [berger1993]. Berger and David Garfinkle showed in 1998 that the nonlinear terms of the wave equations drive $v$ below 1, and that the spiky features form at isolated points of space where those terms are absent [berger1998]. Satyanad Kichenassamy and Alan Rendall proved the same year that, given analytic asymptotic data with $0 < v < 1$, there is a unique solution with those asymptotics, the data being as many functions as the initial value problem needs [kichenassamy1998, ringstrom2010]. Garfinkle's simulations of $S^2 \times S^1$ in 1999 found the same velocity dominated approach almost everywhere [garfinkle1999]. Rendall and Marsha Weaver constructed solutions with spikes in 2001, in some of which the Kretschmann scalar blows up at a rate that varies near the spike [rendall2001].¶Hans Ringström proved in 2006 that every solution on the torus has an asymptotic velocity $v_\infty(\theta)$ at each $\theta$, and that the curvature blows up along every causal curve ending where $v_\infty \neq 1$ [ringstrom2006, ringstrom2010]. At $v_\infty = 1$, the value of the flat Kasner universe, the Kretschmann scalar need not be unbounded [ringstrom2010]. In 2009 he proved strong cosmic censorship for the unpolarised torus: for a set of initial data open in the $C^1 \times C^0$ topology and dense in the $C^\infty$ topology, the spacetime is causally geodesically complete in one time direction, the Kretschmann scalar is unbounded along every inextendible causal curve in the other, and the maximal globally hyperbolic development is $C^2$ inextendible [ringstrom2009, ringstrom2010].

related.text: Gowdy built his universes from Einstein and Rosen's cylindrical waves by changing their boundary conditions [gowdy1971]. Where the gradient of $R$ is spacelike, the $S^3$ and $S^2 \times S^1$ universes transform locally into an Einstein-Rosen wave [gowdy2014].

A Gowdy torus that is the same at every $\theta$: $P = \tau$, $Q = 0$ is the flat Kasner universe [ringstrom2010]. Near the singularity each $\theta$ of a polarised solution approaches a Kasner universe of its own [berger1974].
The Taub universe is a Gowdy spacetime on $S^3$. It can be extended past its Big Bang, which is why strong cosmic censorship is stated for generic initial data [gowdy2014].
Between its outer and inner horizons Kerr's metric is a Gowdy spacetime on $S^2 \times S^1$, with $t$ wrapped into a circle [obregon1998, garfinkle1999].

Obregón and Ryan's Kerr example with the spin switched off [obregon1998]. The inside of Schwarzschild's horizon is a polarised Gowdy spacetime on $S^2 \times S^1$, with $r = L(1 - \cos t)$, $r_s = 2L$, $e^{2a} = (1 - \cos t)^2$, and $e^{P} = (1 - \cos t)^2\sin\theta/\sin t$.

The Kantowski-Sachs universe with no matter is the inside of Schwarzschild's horizon [ellismaccallum1969], and with its axis wrapped into a circle that is a polarised Gowdy spacetime on $S^2 \times S^1$ [obregon1998].

Both are testing grounds for the conjecture of Belinskii, Khalatnikov, and Lifshitz that each small region near a generic singularity evolves as a homogeneous universe of its own [bkl1970]. The Mixmaster universe oscillates all the way down, and in a generic Gowdy universe the spatial curvature terms drop out [gowdy2014].

An inhomogeneous cosmology with the same two commuting symmetries of space, filled with radiation and arranged around an axis. Every geodesic in it runs on for ever, with no singularity at either end of time [ruiz1992, chinea1992].

The same field equations with $\theta$ unrolled into a line. Belinski and Zakharov's inverse scattering method adds solitons to any known solution with these two symmetries, by algebra alone [belinskii1978].
Friedmann's flat universe on the same 3-torus, with matter and no waves. With matter added, the Gowdy universes that are the same at every point include it [martinbenito2011].

parameters.description: Length that sets the scale of the universe ($L > 0$)

Wave amplitude, a dimensionless function of $t$ and $\theta$, periodic in $\theta$; the spacetime is a vacuum exactly where $\partial_t^2P + \dfrac{1}{t}\partial_tP - \partial_\theta^2P = e^{2P}\left(\left(\partial_tQ\right)^2 - \left(\partial_\theta Q\right)^2\right)$ together with the equations for $Q$ and $\lambda$

Twist of the two polarisations, a dimensionless function of $t$ and $\theta$, periodic in $\theta$, with $Q = 0$ the polarised case; in a vacuum $\partial_t^2Q + \dfrac{1}{t}\partial_tQ - \partial_\theta^2Q = -2\left(\partial_tP\,\partial_tQ - \partial_\theta P\,\partial_\theta Q\right)$

Dimensionless function of $t$ and $\theta$, periodic in $\theta$; in a vacuum $\partial_t\lambda = t\left(\left(\partial_tP\right)^2 + \left(\partial_\theta P\right)^2 + e^{2P}\left(\left(\partial_tQ\right)^2 + \left(\partial_\theta Q\right)^2\right)\right)$ and $\partial_\theta\lambda = 2t\left(\partial_tP\,\partial_\theta P + e^{2P}\partial_tQ\,\partial_\theta Q\right)$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, \theta, \sigma, \delta)$ on $T^3$, with $\partial_\sigma$ and $\partial_\delta$ the two Killing vectors and $t$ the area of their orbits in units of $4\pi^2L^2$, which vanishes at the singularity. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

parameters.description: Length that sets the scale of the universe ($L > 0$)

Wave amplitude, a dimensionless function of $\tau$ and $\theta$, periodic in $\theta$; the spacetime is a vacuum exactly where $\partial_\tau^2P - e^{-2\tau}\partial_\theta^2P = e^{2P}\left(\left(\partial_\tau Q\right)^2 - e^{-2\tau}\left(\partial_\theta Q\right)^2\right)$ together with the equations for $Q$ and $\lambda$

Twist of the two polarisations, a dimensionless function of $\tau$ and $\theta$, periodic in $\theta$, with $Q = 0$ the polarised case; in a vacuum $\partial_\tau^2Q - e^{-2\tau}\partial_\theta^2Q = -2\left(\partial_\tau P\,\partial_\tau Q - e^{-2\tau}\partial_\theta P\,\partial_\theta Q\right)$

Dimensionless function of $\tau$ and $\theta$, periodic in $\theta$; in a vacuum $\partial_\tau\lambda = -\left(\partial_\tau P\right)^2 - e^{-2\tau}\left(\partial_\theta P\right)^2 - e^{2P}\left(\left(\partial_\tau Q\right)^2 + e^{-2\tau}\left(\partial_\theta Q\right)^2\right)$ and $\partial_\theta\lambda = -2\left(\partial_\tau P\,\partial_\theta P + e^{2P}\partial_\tau Q\,\partial_\theta Q\right)$

coordinates.convention: We use the time $\tau = -\ln t$ of the areal chart, which grows toward the past and reaches $+\infty$ at the singularity, with $\theta$, $\sigma$, and $\delta$ as in that chart. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

Dimensionless function of $t$ and $\theta$; in a vacuum $\cot\theta\,\partial_ta + \cot t\,\partial_\theta a = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\cot t\cot\theta + \partial_tP\,\partial_\theta P + e^{2P}\partial_tQ\,\partial_\theta Q\right)$ and $\cot t\,\partial_ta + \cot\theta\,\partial_\theta a = \dfrac{1}{4}\left(\left(\partial_tP\right)^2 + \left(\partial_\theta P\right)^2 + e^{2P}\left(\left(\partial_tQ\right)^2 + \left(\partial_\theta Q\right)^2\right) - \cot^2t - \cot^2\theta\right) - 1$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, \theta, \sigma, \delta)$ on $S^3$ and on $S^2 \times S^1$, with $\partial_\sigma$ and $\partial_\delta$ the two Killing vectors, whose orbits have area $4\pi^2L^2\sin t\sin\theta$ and shrink to the rotation axes at $\theta = 0$ and $\theta = \pi$. The universe begins at $t = 0$ and ends at $t = \pi$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.
